passage: I'm Asif, and I've never been that loud in my life. Last month's final: India needed six runs off the last over, and eight of us were crammed on Karthik's sofa. I couldn't sit. My heart was hammering like I was the one holding the bat. Karthik was chewing his collar. When the fifth ball went for four, I grabbed his arm so hard he yelped. Last ball, two to win. Nobody breathed. When it went over the fence, we all jumped at once, and Karthik's mother came running, thinking the ceiling fan had fallen. I was hugging people I barely knew. My voice was gone for two days. Weird, right? I wasn't even on the field. But it felt like my win too.

qa.q: How many people were crammed on Karthik's sofa?
qa.a: Eight of us were crammed on the sofa.

qa.q: Why was Asif's heart hammering during the last over?
qa.a: Asif was so tense and excited that the match felt personal, as if Asif were the one batting.

qa.q: If Asif wanted that shared joy again, what could Asif plan, and why would it work?
qa.a: Asif could gather friends to watch the next big match together, since feeling the tension and the win alongside others made it so strong.

qa.q: How might Karthik's mother see the jumping and shouting?
qa.a: Karthik's mother was alarmed at first, thinking the fan had fallen, but may later enjoy seeing the friends so joyful together. 😊

grounding: A teenager feels a cricket final's last over as if batting personally, sharing wild joy with friends.

passage: Film club note, Friday. Bhavna Joshi, teacher in charge. We screened the old film about a girl who runs away to join a football team. At the climax, the penalty shootout, I watched Minakshi (Class 9) more than the screen. She was gripping the armrests, lips moving, rocking forward with every kick. When the heroine missed, she gasped as if she'd been hit. When the final goal went in, she jumped up and hugged Farida beside her, laughing and crying. Half the room had done the same. Afterwards she said, 'Ma'am, my heart is still running.' Next: I'll ask the club to write about why a story can feel as if it's happening to us, and we'll choose next month's film together.

qa.a: A penalty shootout.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's "my heart is still running" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Minakshi lived the story as if it were her own, feeling the tension and joy in her body.

qa.a: Writing about why stories feel personal helps students understand that strong feeling, and choosing the next film together keeps the shared joy going.

qa.a: Farida, who may have felt the same thrill, probably enjoyed sharing the joy right there with Minakshi.

passage:
Sunday
I still can't sleep. Elizabeth and I went to watch the state women's hockey final at the stadium, our district against the champions. I don't even play hockey! But when it went to extra time, my heart was banging so hard I thought people could hear it. I bit the end of Elizabeth's dupatta. I actually prayed. When our striker scored in the last minute, the whole stand went up like one body, and I screamed words that aren't words. Elizabeth was crying. A lady behind us hugged us both.
On the bus home everybody was singing, even strangers. I didn't know you could feel that happy about something that wasn't even yours. Except it felt like ours.
— Salma

qa.q: Who hugged Salma and Elizabeth?
qa.a: The lady behind them hugged them both.

qa.q: Why did the win feel like "ours" to Salma, who doesn't even play hockey?
qa.a: Salma felt thrilled and connected to the team and the crowd, so the win felt personal, shared with everyone there.

qa.a: Salma could go to more local matches with Elizabeth, or join a club, since being part of a crowd behind a team clearly lifts Salma's spirits.

qa.q: What might the win mean to the strangers singing on the bus?
qa.a: For them the win was a shared joy too, turning a bus full of people who didn't know each other into one celebrating group.

grounding: A teenager who doesn't play hockey feels a state final as if it were personal and shares the joy with a whole crowd.

passage:
The gram panchayat had hired a projector for the women's cricket final, and half the village of Kherwadi sat on durries in the school ground. Indu, fifteen, squeezed between her brother Vaibhav and the old postman.
In the last over the team needed nine runs. Indu found she was gripping Vaibhav's wrist so hard he winced. Her own mouth was dry, her knees jumping. When the batter swung and the ball flew, Indu was on her feet before it landed, and so was everyone else, the postman too, his cap falling off.
"Six!" someone yelled. Two balls later, a four, and the ground exploded. Strangers hugged her. A grandmother Indu had never spoken to kissed her forehead.
Walking home under the stars, Indu's legs still trembled. "I didn't even hit the ball," she said. Vaibhav laughed. "You nearly broke my wrist hitting it."

qa.q: Where was the final shown?
qa.a: It was shown on a projector in the school ground.

qa.q: Why were Indu's legs still trembling on the walk home?
qa.a: She had felt the last over as if she were playing, with a dry mouth and jumping knees, and the thrill had not left her body yet.

qa.q: What made this final such a strong experience for Indu, and what could she choose to do with that?
qa.a: Watching with the whole village turned her own pounding heart into shared joy; she could seek out more matches with others, or even ask to join a local team.

qa.q: How did the old postman seem to experience the moment?
qa.a: He jumped up with everyone, cap falling off, showing that the win swept up older villagers too, not just the young.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose heart pounds through a cricket final as if it were her own game, and how feeling it with others gives strong shared joy.
